--- Page 1 ---
LLM Evolutionary Search Strategies Should be Compared by Tokens
Tal Oved*
Roi Pony
Oshri Naparstek
Udi Barzelay
IBM Research
Abstract
LLM evolutionary search is currently evaluated
by counting proposals (candidate programs).
We demonstrate this metric hides the true cost
of search, and redo the comparison using to-
kens. By replaying 600 logged runs across 5
tasks and 3 methods, we show that proposal
costs vary wildly from 16k to 39k tokens. In
equal-proposal comparisons, this silently grants
some methods up to 1.9× the compute of oth-
ers, and gives evolution roughly 6× the budget
of independent sampling. When we match to-
ken budgets, giving sampling six times more
attempts, and remove scorer exploits, the evolu-
tionary advantage largely vanishes. Evolution
beats independent sampling by 5% or less on 12
of 15 task-method pairs, retaining a 23 to 28%
margin on only 3, all on one task. A replication
with Claude Haiku 4.5 reproduces this split,
though a third backbone shows its size depends
on the model too. The performance margin
justifying these systems is often an accounting
artifact. Reporting tokens, not proposals and
not model calls, fixes this and costs nothing, as
the logs already hold them.
1
Introduction
Large language models now serve as the proposal
step in evolutionary search over programs. A model
writes a candidate, an evaluator scores it, the best
are kept, and the model is asked to edit them
again. The results are strong enough to change
what counts as a discovery method. FunSearch
found new mathematical constructions this way
(Romera-Paredes et al., 2024), AlphaEvolve ex-
tended the loop to algorithms and hardware kernels
(Novikov et al., 2025), and open engines such as
OpenEvolve reproduce it for public use (Sharma,
2025). The same loop drives heuristic design (Liu
et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024), prompt optimization
(Fernando et al., 2023; Agrawal et al., 2026), and
*Corresponding author: Tal.Oved@ibm.com
sample-efficient variants (Lange et al., 2026), and
ADRS-Bench collects systems-optimization tasks
for the setting (Cheng et al., 2025).
These runs are reported in proposals, meaning
candidate programs: a search is k seeds grown for
t iterations, and methods are compared at matched
kt. Oved et al. (2026) showed that how a fixed bud-
get is split between k and t changes which method
appears to win. Our concern is the unit itself. A
proposal is not a fixed amount of compute, because
an evolve prompt carries the current program and
part of the archive and both grow as the run pro-
ceeds. A later proposal therefore costs more than
an earlier one, and a method that shows the model
more context costs more per proposal. Cost-aware
controllers already assume this (Zhang et al., 2026;
Ishibashi et al., 2026), and what is missing is the
measurement of what a proposal costs, and of what
it does to a published comparison once that com-
parison is paid for in tokens.
These systems are usually validated against an
ablation that removes evolution and samples pro-
grams independently, run at equal proposals. Inde-
pendent sampling is a serious competitor at scale
(Brown et al., 2024; Snell et al., 2024; Beck et al.,
2026). If one proposal costs several times what
one sample costs, that ablation got a fraction of
the compute it should have had, and the reported
margin is partly an artifact of the accounting.
In this work, we measure both sides. We re-
play 600 logged runs over 5 optimization tasks and
3 search strategies, re-indexing every best-so-far
curve against cumulative tokens. One proposal
costs 16k to 39k tokens depending on strategy and
task, so on one task an equal-proposal comparison
can hand one strategy 1.9× the compute of another.
One proposal costs about six times one indepen-
dent sample. Paid the same number of tokens, so
that sampling gets roughly six times more attempts,
evolution wins by 5% or less on 12 of our 15 strat-
egy and task pairs, one of them indistinguishable
1
arXiv:2610.23977v1  [cs.NE]  13 Oct 2026


--- Page 2 ---
from parity, and by 23 to 28% on the other 3.
Validity inspection.
On transaction scheduling
the best program scored 5× the baseline by placing
3 of 300 transactions, and the scorer accepted it.
Scorers that can be gamed are a known problem
(Liu et al., 2023; Aleithan et al., 2024; Lehman
et al., 2020; Skalse et al., 2022), and taking the
maximum over many runs is how you find the ex-
ploits (Stroebl et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2021).
So we re-run the programs on both sides and score
them under the same coverage rule.
Contributions.
• A token-level accounting of LLM evolution-
ary search: what one proposal costs per strat-
egy and per task, and how far that is from one
independent sample (§4).
• The comparison against independent sampling
redone at equal token cost, with exact order
statistics on both sides (§4).
• A re-execution audit of candidate programs
that removes a 5× headline result and erases
the ranking it created on that task (§4).
Related work.
Oved et al. (2026), a concurrent
work, asks how to split a fixed kt budget between
seeds and depth; it takes the proposal as the unit, or-
thogonal to what we test. Zhang et al. (2026) price
search actions inside a controller to spend a token
budget well. They assert the cost spread; we mea-
sure it. Ishibashi et al. (2026) also fix a token bud-
get and report that deeper reasoning per candidate
beats more candidates, on one task and with evolu-
tion on both sides of every comparison. Gupta et al.
(2026) vary harness components budget-matched
and find no configuration that wins everywhere,
with no sampling arm and no program audit. Beck
et al. (2026) argue archives and frameworks can be
dropped in favor of sampling edits to the best veri-
fied solution, though their sampler is conditioned
on that incumbent and compute is reported in wall-
clock time, not tokens. Rajan (2026) measures how
often a code RL environment accepts an incorrect
solution; we measure the realized exploit inside
a search population, where selection amplifies it.
Reward hacking and specification gaming are long-
standing concerns (Amodei et al., 2016; Krakovna
et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2022).
2
Experimental Setup
Engine, models and strategies.
All runs use
the ADRS engine (Cheng et al., 2025) with
gpt-5-mini; model, objective and evaluator re-
main fixed to isolate the search strategy. The three
strategies are OpenEvolve (islands plus archive,
population 40; Sharma, 2025), EvoX (co-evolves
its selection rule; Liu et al., 2026a) and AdaEvolve
(adaptive variant; Cemri et al., 2026). Each task-
strategy cell runs extensively for 40 independent
seeds and 200 iterations, a budget of 8,000 propos-
als per cell, for 600 logged runs. Throughout, a run
is one seed and a cell is the forty runs of one task-
strategy pair. Every run logs one line per model call
with its prompt, completion and reasoning token
counts, and one row per evaluated program with its
score and a timestamp, which is what lets us price
the search afterwards.
Tasks and baseline.
We use three system tasks
from ADRS-Bench (Cheng et al., 2025): PRISM,
an LLM-serving scheduler measured by goodput;
Cloudcast, a broadcast planner measured by trans-
fer cost; and transaction scheduling, measured by
throughput. We add two mathematical construc-
tion tasks, circle packing in a square and the Heil-
bronn triangle problem, giving five tasks, fifteen
cells. Each task is optimized through its native
combined_score. Against these we run a sam-
pling baseline: 8,000 independent programs drawn
from the task description alone, with no history or
archive, scored by the same evaluator. This is the
control used in prior work (Oved et al., 2026); our
contribution is to charge both sides the same way.
3
Method
Notation.
Seed i of a cell produces candidates
with scores f(xi,1), . . . , f(xi,t), and its value at
depth t is the running best
Mi(t) = max
1≤s≤t f(xi,s).
(1)
Running k seeds and keeping the best gives
Bk(t) = maxi≤k Mi(t). Prior work budgets this
by proposals, B = k t.
Pricing a run.
The two logs share one clock, so
the tokens a seed has spent by the time its j-th
program appears is the cumulative sum over the
model calls that precede it. Every seed therefore
becomes a curve of best score against tokens spent
rather than against iterations. Summing over the
2


--- Page 3 ---
calls, and not over the proposals, matters because a
proposal is not one call: retries and the occasional
meta-call that a strategy makes to steer itself are
charged here and are invisible in a proposal count.
Comparing at equal cost.
Given a token budget
B, we let k seeds share it and read each seed’s
curve at B/k, then take the best over k and maxi-
mize over k. Which k of the 40 seeds a practitioner
draws is averaged out with exact order statistics, so
no number depends on one ordering and there is no
resampling noise. The baseline is priced the same
way: a budget buys B over the cost per sample, and
the expected best of that many is again an exact or-
der statistic. We cap every budget at what the sam-
pling pool covers, between 28 and 48 million to-
kens, preventing extrapolation. We report proposal-
budget and token-budget comparisons side by side,
isolating accounting from search.
Auditing the programs.
Three of these scorers
accept programs that fail the task, and two of them
can only be caught by running the program again,
so we re-execute those and check coverage directly:
for transaction scheduling, how many of the 300
transactions a schedule places, and for Cloudcast,
the fraction of required partitions that arrive. Both
sides are judged by identical code. Because such a
program can lead midway through a run, we walk
each seed in order, keep the best score surviving
the check, and re-execute a candidate only when it
would beat it, about six re-runs per seed versus two
hundred. Where logs already record coverage, as
PRISM does, we read it from them.
4
Results
A proposal is not a unit of compute.
Figure 1
and Table 1 demonstrate it. One proposal costs
23.0k tokens under OpenEvolve, 27.0k under EvoX
and 33.9k under AdaEvolve, and between 15.6k
and 38.6k across cells, a spread of 2.5×. One pro-
posal also takes 1.3 to 1.8 model calls on average,
because retries and extra calls some methods make
to steer themselves are not proposals. Reasoning
tokens are 5 to 24% of a proposal.
Appendix C repeats this on Haiku 4.5, over two
math tasks and all three strategies at the same 40
seeds by 200 iterations. AdaEvolve remains dear-
est, where OpenEvolve is 41% cheaper per pro-
posal for one task and 9% dearer for the other.
Two consequences.
Across tasks, an equal-
proposal comparison gives AdaEvolve 1.5×

Table 1: Cost of one proposal, averaged over tasks,
against the cost of one independent sample. Reasoning
tokens are a share of the total. The sample column is a
range because it varies by task.
OpenEvolve’s compute, and in one task reaching
1.9×, so part of any reported advantage is a larger
budget. One cell, forty runs by 200 iterations, costs
108–309 million tokens, averaging 194 million, no-
table in a field reporting iteration counts.
Sampling is roughly six times cheaper per at-
tempt.
An independent sample costs 4.1k to 6.0k
tokens, against 16k to 39k for a proposal (Fig-
ure 1). The ratio is 4.6× on circle packing, 4.8×
on PRISM, 5.8× on Cloudcast, 6.0× on Heilbronn
and 7.2× on transaction scheduling, a mean of
5.7×. The cause is structural: an evolve prompt
carries the program being edited and part of the
archive, and both grow as the run proceeds, while
a fresh sample carries only the task description.
This matters since most works in the field, run
this baseline at equal proposals. At equal tokens it
should get more attempts than it was given.
At equal cost, evolution wins less.
Table 2 gives
both sides at two budget definitions, and Figure 2
in Appendix B plots the full curves. The correction
comes first. At equal proposals the largest advan-
tage was transaction scheduling with AdaEvolve at
5.06×; that cell’s winner places 3 of 300 transac-
tions. it reads 5.06 in both currencies, because its
exploit is found early and cheaply, leaving nothing
for more tokens. Auditing all three methods on that
task drops the equal-token ratio from 5.06 to 1.02
for AdaEvolve, from 1.14 to 1.02 for OpenEvolve,
leaving EvoX untouched at 1.04 because its forty
winners place every transaction.
What remains is small; intervals agree: only
Cloudcast with OpenEvolve spans parity, PRISM’s
three sit just above, and only Heilbronn’s exceed
1.17 (Table 7). The largest advantages are all Heil-
bronn, 1.23–1.28 across methods, and on PRISM
all three land within 1%. Moving from equal pro-
posals to equal tokens removes some advantage in
12 of 15 pairs, excepting the three PRISM pairs al-
ready at parity, and on Cloudcast with OpenEvolve

Figure 1: Tokens per proposal, by method and task, with the independent sample cost as the dashed line. Equal-
proposal comparisons yield equal compute only if these bars match, which they do not: the same method varies by
up to 2.4× across tasks, and within a task the methods differ by up to 1.9×. The distance to the dashed line (4.6×
to 7.2×) is why a sampling baseline run at equal proposals is given far less compute than the compared methods.
removes it all, leaving sampling ahead. Count-
ing model calls instead does not fix it either (Ap-
pendix F). Reporting in proposals flatters evolution
twice: once by not charging for larger prompts, and
again if nobody checks its best program’s output.
The final sample doubling yields +0.00% on
circle packing, +0.38% on PRISM, +0.44% on
transaction scheduling, +1.37% on Heilbronn and
+3.63% on Cloudcast. Sampling has saturated here
while evolution still rises, so the window favours
sampling and reported margins are lower bounds.
Scorer exploits, and what removing them costs.
Reward hacking is well documented; we treat it as
a filter, reporting changes (Table 9). Three of five
scorers accept programs skipping most of the task,
and one accepts a working program that misreports.
Two exploits win here, and selection spreads both:
in the worst transaction-scheduling seed, the top 69
distinct programs are identical exploits, and over
a third of candidates score there. Cloudcast’s sim-
ulator prices plans from submitted edge data, not
the provided network, so plans passing coverage
checks are billed a fraction of true cost; re-running
reproduces this faithfully, so only graph compar-
isons catch it. One topped the Cloudcast EvoX
cell, dropping it from 1.08 to 1.05. PRISM is gated
throughout, so degenerate winners never reach our
numbers, though an ungated best-of-k would ship
one under all three methods. Circle packing and
Heilbronn validate outputs, serving as controls.
5
Conclusion
Report tokens alongside proposals. The logs al-
ready hold them; without them an equal-proposal
comparison can vary by 1.9× in compute between

methods on one task and by about 6× from the

Paid in tokens and audited, evolutionary search
beat independent sampling by 5% or less on 12
of 15 pairs, and by 23–28% on the other 3, all
Heilbronn. The difference was the task rather than
the method. Heilbronn has a long improvement
path where editing a good program keeps paying;
on the other four tasks a fresh sample is almost as
4


--- Page 5 ---
good for a fraction of the cost. So check whether a
task rewards search before choosing a searcher.
Audit both sides, and record audit requirements
during the run. One stored coverage number per
candidate would replace every re-execution here.
Limitations
Logging and evaluating every API call across 1,200
full runs imposes a heavy compute cost, which
practically limits studies to fewer tasks and search
methods. Therefore, we report fifteen pairs, not a
broad distribution. The main comparison uses one
backbone, with a second in Appendix C on the two
math tasks, where the same task-dependent split
appears, and with a third in Appendix D on the
three system tasks.
The comparison window is capped by the size of
the sampling pool, so evolution is measured using
about a fifth of its logged corpus. Its curves are
still rising there, so the window favours sampling
and our margins are lower bounds. This pool size
is partly constrained by task difficulty: Cloudcast,
for example, rejects a large portion of independent
samples, with 38% of draws returning an error and
no score, leaving 4,898 usable programs out of
8,000.
Finally, prices are reported as token counts, not
dollars, because per-token prices change; a reader
can simply multiply by the current rate.
Ethical considerations
The primary ethical dimension of this work is com-
putational and environmental cost. LLM evolution-
ary search demands a substantial energy footprint,
requiring tens of thousands of API calls per run.
Our methodology mitigates this by analyzing exist-
ing logged runs rather than executing new searches,
maximizing the utility of already-expended com-
pute. Furthermore, by demonstrating that indepen-
dent sampling can often match evolutionary search
at a fraction of the token budget, our findings en-
courage more energy-efficient uses of language
models. The datasets and tasks evaluate system
optimization and mathematics, presenting no risks
regarding human subjects, privacy, or demographic
bias.

A
Implementation details
All experiments run on SkyDiscover (Liu et al.,
2026b), an open framework for AI-driven algorith-
mic discovery, using its strategy implementations,
task evaluators, and logging. Building on it keeps
our pipeline reproducible.
B
Score against tokens spent
Figure 2 plots the curves behind Table 2, one panel
per task: best score so far against cumulative to-
kens, for each search method and for independent
sampling on the same axis.

using the ablation runs on the two math tasks at
the same 40 seeds by 200 iterations, all six cells
complete. Table 3 and Figure 3 give the result,
and the main point is how little changes from the

Figure 2: Best score against tokens spent. Solid lines are evolutionary search, one per method, each at its own best
number of seeds for that budget. Cloudcast is shown with its coverage gate applied to both sides, and with the two
cells whose ceiling misreported its transfer price capped at their best valid program. The dashed line is independent
sampling, which at the same budget gets five to seven times more attempts, depending on the task. The transaction
scheduling curves are shown after the audit: each seed is capped at the best program that places all 300 transactions
and the three exploit seeds are dropped, so that panel tops out near 4,400 rather than 21,277. The range stops where
the sampling pool stops, so nothing is extrapolated.
first engine model. Costs land in the same band
on both backbones rather than tracking the model:
on circle packing EvoX and AdaEvolve are within
3% of their gpt-5-mini values, on Heilbronn within
13% and 19%, and only OpenEvolve moves far,
41% cheaper on circle packing and 9% dearer on
Heilbronn. What does transfer cleanly is that AdaE-
volve is dearest everywhere, on both tasks and both
backbones. The one ordering that does not sur-
vive is OpenEvolve being cheapest: on Haiku Heil-
bronn EvoX edges it, 19,275 against 19,645. So the
spread we report in Section 4 is closer to a property
of the harness than of the model, without being a
fixed ranking.
On circle packing one AdaEvolve proposal costs
2.7× one OpenEvolve proposal, against 1.6× for
the same pair on gpt-5-mini. An equal-proposal
comparison is therefore no safer on a cheaper
model. One difference worth noting: Haiku reports
no reasoning tokens at all, on any of the 58,615
calls in these six cells, where gpt-5-mini spends 5
to 24% of a proposal on them.

of-N pool for each task: 8,000 attempts, of which

D
A third backbone: the systems tasks
Appendix C covers the two math tasks on a sec-
ond backbone. This one covers the three systems
tasks on gemini-2.5-flash, all three strategies
and a best-of-N pool each, at the same forty seeds
by 200 iterations. Everything here is gated and
audited exactly as in Table 2: PRISM on success
rate, Cloudcast on coverage and on declared price,
transaction scheduling by re-execution. That au-
dit found no transaction-scheduling exploit on this
backbone, all 118 winners placing every transac-
tion, and three Cloudcast winners that misreport
their price.
Table 5 demonstrates that the accounting prob-
lem can be worse. One proposal costs 16.8k to-
kens in the cheapest cell and 65.4k in the dearest,
a 3.9× spread against 2.5× on gpt-5-mini, so
an equal-proposal comparison misallocates more
on this model. Little of the ordering carries over:
AdaEvolve moves from 1.3× to 2.5× the cost of
OpenEvolve, while transaction scheduling with
EvoX becomes 29% cheaper rather than dearer.
Reasoning is a third to two thirds of a proposal,
against 5 to 24% before. One independent sample
costs 2.1 to 2.6× more as well, so the gap between
a proposal and a sample narrows to 3.3–4.4×.
Table 6 gives the comparison. Evolution wins
by more on this backbone: the mean ratio is 1.30
at equal tokens against 1.07 on gpt-5-mini, and
Cloudcast moves from about parity to 1.53–1.59.
Pricing in tokens still only reduces the advantage,
from 1.31 to 1.30. What does not hold is that
the size of the margin belongs to the task alone:
the same task pays very differently on a different
model. The unit is wrong on both backbones; how
much search is worth is not settled by either.
E
Confidence intervals
The intervals in Table 7 come from 2,000 repli-
cates that resample both sides: a cell’s forty seed
curves, with replacement, and the sampling pool,
with replacement. The ratio is recomputed in each
replicate, so the interval covers the finite seed pool
and the finite draw pool together. In three cells the
best seed count is forty, which makes the statistic a
sample maximum, where the bootstrap is not con-
sistent; those use subsampling instead, m = 20
of 40 without replacement, whose spread is wider
than the true forty-seed spread and so cannot under-
state the interval. It moves one bound, Heilbronn
with OpenEvolve from 1.18 to 1.17.
F
Budgeting by model calls
Once proposals are shown not to be a unit of com-
pute, the natural fallback is to count API calls. That
fails for the same reason: an evolve prompt carries
the program being edited and part of the archive,
and both grow as the run proceeds, so a later call is
a larger call. Figure 6 shows it directly. Tokens per
call run from 12.4k in the cheapest cell to 28.1k in
the dearest, a 2.3× spread against 2.5× for tokens
per proposal, so calls remove about a twelfth of the
variation. One evolve call costs 3.3 to 4.4× one
sampling call, against 4.7 to 7.2× per proposal.
Table 8 repeats Table 2 with a call budget beside
the other two. On the sampling side one call is one
draw, so a budget of B calls buys B draws; on the
evolve side the cumulative call count replaces cu-

Table 9: What each scorer accepts, how often it happens,
and what removing it costs. The Degenerate column
counts seeds whose own best program fails a direct
coverage check, out of the seeds we re-executed; both
Cloudcast rows rest on the same 113, because seven
of its winners cannot be re-run at all. Circle packing
and Heilbronn accept nothing because their evaluators
validate the output themselves, the latter rejecting any
result that does not place every point inside the triangle.
The Effect column is the change to Table 2: transaction
scheduling loses its headline, Cloudcast is unaffected
by the two that send no partitions because neither ever
led, but one of the two that misreport their price was a
cell ceiling, and PRISM’s gate excludes its own before
they are scored.
